summary: Omniscope is an interactive web platform for the NASA Space Apps Challenge that makes SPHEREx infrared sky data accessible to everyone. Our website empowers users to explore the universe and view detailed information on coordinated celestial objects. It features intuitive Swipe, Blink, and Difference comparison modes, alongside dynamic time-lapse videos of the evolving night sky. These tools help users easily track moving cosmic bodies, analyze specific coordinates, and search for distant anomalies like Planet X. By turning complex datasets into a visual, user-friendly experience, we invite citizen scientists everywhere to uncover hidden cosmic wonders.
details:
OmniScope is Team OmniScope’s submission for the NASA Space Apps Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It’s a public web tool that lets anyone replay the same patch of sky using real infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Our goal is to make it easier for students, educators, and citizen scientists to explore how the sky changes over time.

Visitors can choose a target such as Barnard’s Star or enter their own right ascension and declination in decimal degrees. OmniScope retrieves FITS images from NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), aligns them to a common sky grid, and puts them on a timeline. Users can play the sequence, jump to a date, compare images side by side, blink between visits, or view a difference image. Find Movers flags possible changes when enough comparable observations are available. Those flags give users a place to start investigating.

What makes OmniScope distinctive is the connection between the image and where SPHEREx was when it took it. The 3D Earth view shows the spacecraft’s recorded position for the selected exposure and offers a separate estimate of its current orbit. Users can also filter by infrared wavelength, stack exposures, inspect a source’s spectrum, and turn on Gaia DR3 or AllWISE overlays for context. Share links reopen the same sky field and display settings.

We built OmniScope with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js. GitHub Pages hosts the interface, and a Cloudflare Worker proxies live data requests. The project uses NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx and AllWISE data, NASA JPL Horizons for planetary positions, ESA’s Gaia Archive for Gaia DR3, CDS Sesame for name lookup, and CelesTrak orbital elements with satellite.js for the orbit estimate.

We considered ease of use, archive response times, and how to avoid mistaking artifacts for astronomical changes. Bundled observations let users start exploring while live data loads. The viewer labels the data release date separately from the date the image was taken, and offers quality masks and detector information to help users compare images responsibly.
